claims.text: The starting material is single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a single-phase fcc FeCoNi-based high-entropy-alloy derivative.
Thermal annealing can induce precipitation or formation of a secondary phase in FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys.
The annealing-induced secondary phase will be Co-rich.
Annealing at 500–700°C for 1–10 hours is an appropriate process window for producing the proposed precipitates.
The Co-rich precipitated phase has a high magnetocrystalline anisotropy constant.
A secondary phase with high magnetocrystalline anisotropy can act as a domain-wall pinning site.
Domain-wall pinning increases the energy required for domain-wall motion.
The increased resistance to domain-wall motion increases coercive field.
The intervention will increase coercive field by at least a factor of five relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy-alloy derivative.
The proposed baseline materials have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe.
The hypothesis is restricted to FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys having no more than 10% deviation from equiatomic composition.
The post-intervention structure consists of an fcc host structure containing a secondary phase.
The predicted coercivity change applies to magnetic measurements performed at room temperature.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on annealing conditions, composition, and microstructure.
Failure of every annealed sample to reach a fivefold coercivity increase relative to the baseline is designated as falsification of the hypothesis.
